summary: Privately owned memorial-style tower near Hansville, Puget Sound, topped with the lantern room from Smith Island Light; a fixed-red aid since 1965.

lens.note: Replica fourth-order lens installed 2021; the original Smith Island lens is at the Museum of History and Industry, Seattle

structures.note: About 30 ft (LighthouseFriends/Salish Sea). Lantern room from Smith Island Lighthouse. Built by Jim Gibbs; the date is disputed (1959, 1963 or 1964).

staffing.note: No keeper's quarters and no keepers listed (archive)

access.note: Privately owned by the Skunk Bay Lighthouse Association. Grounds, dwelling and tower closed; no access allowed (Salish Sea Lighthouses). Do not land or climb.

stay.note: Members only: each share includes a one-week stay each quarter (LighthouseFriends)

events.note: Construction by Jim Gibbs, dated 1959 by LighthouseFriends; Salish Sea Lighthouses gives 1964; HistoryLink's 1963 report is an earlier date for the lantern room at the site
Lantern room already at Skunk Bay, per a 1963 Seattle Times article as cited by HistoryLink
Changed to fixed red and reduced in power after a Coast Guard inspection; operational as a private aid to navigation since
About twenty people formed the Skunk Bay Lighthouse Association and bought the structure
Enlarged building (bedrooms, bathroom, living and dining room, loft) dedicated
Replica fourth-order Fresnel lens installed; ownership given to the U.S. Lighthouse Society

corrections.why: The record's 1965 matches the year of the change to a fixed red light (LighthouseFriends), not a construction date given by any source read. Needs a human look.
The lens at the station is a replica; the Smith Island original is at the Museum of History and Industry in Seattle.
Salish Sea Lighthouses gives the tower's height as 30 feet, about 9 m; no source read here gives a focal height of 64 m. Check the light-list source.

notes_for_editor: 1) Build date disputed: 1959 (LighthouseFriends), 1964 (Salish Sea Lighthouses), and a 1963 Seattle Times report that the lantern was already at the site (HistoryLink; the article was not read). 1965 is the year of the fixed-red change (LighthouseFriends); the record's 1965 'built' comes from Wikidata and is not matched by a source read here. 2) Lens: HistoryLink credits the Puget Sound Historical Maritime Society with salvaging the Smith Island lens; Salish Sea credits Gibbs with rescuing the lantern and lens in 1964. Both say the Smith Island lens is at MOHAI. 3) The record's focal height 64 m (ENC) is not matched by any source read; the tower is about 30 ft per Salish Sea. 4) Private aid: the archive says 'Private Aid: No' and 'Active Aid to Navigation: Yes'; LighthouseFriends says the light operates under the Coast Guard's rules for private aids. The story now states both in its Today section; not resolved. 5) Association members are not named; LighthouseFriends names two members who commissioned the 2021 lens. They are private residents of a converted structure, and their donation is described without names. 6) Not checked: the Coast Guard light list entry for LLNR 6-16545 (not in the local data), the 1963 Seattle Times article, and Gibbs's 1986 book 'Lighthouse of the Pacific' (not accessible). 7) No Coast Guard or Board primary record for this station was found; the story rests on secondary sources. 8) Wikipedia (Smith Island Light) appeared in search and was not cited. 9) Fact-check 2026-10-27: 'built as a memorial light' was LighthouseFriends' label, not a stated purpose, and is now attributed to it. Footnotes for the permission and lens-rescue claims point to LighthouseFriends and Salish Sea; HistoryLink is cited only for the 1963 Seattle Times account and the PSHMS and MOHAI lens. The association's commissioning of the lens is cited to LighthouseFriends alone (the archive does not say it).
